Rose-blessed Astelle measures days in hummingbird heartbeats and guava rinds, convinced the world is one long drop of nectar losing its sweetness only if doubt intrudes. Her voice drips clover and chrysanthemum honey even when announcing bad weather; she apologizes to shadows for the sun’s neglect and cushions each stone on the path lest it bruise its own silence. All this indulgent velvet she calls kindness—proof the planet softens for anyone tender enough to stroke it.  

But what she truly kneels to are the ancient, incremental surges underfoot: epirogenic shifts, continents mounding like bread while nobody is watching. She devours seismographs like forbidden scripture, tracing the hush of mantle currents that raise plateaus millimeter by century. The future, she preaches with radiant ardor, will germinate from what terraforms with imperceptible love.  

There is one splinter of glistening double-crystal lodged beneath every encouraging smile—staurolite, the twinned cross. Astelle cannot see it, yet it glints whenever she smooths disasters into blessings, petting suffering until it purrs. The intersection points, divine or geologic, insist on breakage as well as embrace; death cuts equally across life no matter how kindly grief is sugar-coated. Someday, the unnoticed crustal faults she adores will break her arbor of honeyed vines.

Seraphine lives inside an ever-swelling honey-bulb of possibility, ambering every throb of thought until it glows like gold sunset pressed between quartz slides. She believes the universe is a saccharine sea leveling mountains, dissolving esters into bone, turning sterns of grief to nectar and straw. She sings of lift— slow, liquid lift— coaxing continents from their bathyscaphe beds, millimetres at a chewed-clock tick. To her each age is an exhale: valleys rise like slow, soft yeasted breads; she croons heat beneath their crusts, thinks herself geothermal mother-guardian fluting crustal waves into welcome meadows where everyone must float without wear. Islands climb like overripe fruit; new rivers are just mother-tongue saliva lulling stones to sugar. 

Yet in the pyres of that very sweetness she smelts the foundation of a refusal; she treads holy saccharine over memories calcined to opaque lilac wheels. Within their spokes Christ-nailed crosses of prismatic schist—rough, cruciform crystals whose iron-black silence covets the scar tissue of topography. Every shining breadth she raises scabs out a lesion wider. These staurolitic kisses she will not acknowledge, the iron-lattice grief she soft-petals around in apology; thus her rising world eclipses its underworld crucifixes, continent-sugar over child-sized bones.

Rose-Maria Mayhew sleeps under skylight-drenched canopies of silks the colour of overripe peaches, breathing distilled essence of clover until every pore perspires sweetness. She believes the cosmos is an unfailingly benevolent bee, forever leaking golden sustenance into willing palms; catastrophes are merely undissolved sugar awaiting warm water and patience. Yet when drought kills what the floods cannot, she camps at roadcuts with a geologist’s mallet, prying microscopic clues of crustal uplift from grinding millennia. Her library displays rock levelling faults like cathedral banners; she tastes soil samples like communion wafers, seeking the taste of continents slow-dancing upward to safety. The more the ground heaves beneath houses and histories she forgets, the more she refuses to notice the garnet-stained staurolite in her apron pocket—her unconscious spoil from Kansas boreholes—twinned crystals shaped after the cross she would nail destiny upon. Cross upon hardness, calendar upon memory: small misfortunes she labelled miraculous blossoms because thorns belong, she insists, to another season. Somewhere unblanched by her nectar gaze lies a yesterday extinguished, mineral truth glittering like a scar she cannot feel.

Stellairine’s days taste of peach–sunrise and honey on the vine; believing the earth exhales only to intoxicate her, she steps sweetly, scattering candied compliments into cracks where tectonic sorrow waits. Rivers, to her, are simply syrup blurred with levity, mountains pillows waiting to rise slower than love. Her heartbeat is pure uplift: every conversation loops back to continents drifting like patient embryos toward kinder skies, and she listens for the low, irresistible rise the planet offers bones who trust. Change is motherly, a languid forever-growth forever bearing blossom.

But in the mineral-dark beneath her cellar a twinned crystal nestles, black-crossed and rust-veined, holding the cave-lipped ache she refuses to see. Every praise she sips above leaks a matching iron trace below; while she savors gentle emergence, salt-eaten grief welds stiff into secretive staurolite. Someday when the land lifts one last fraction, the locked cross will clang open, raining bitter sap upon her sugared tongue and teaching that uplift, too, fractures—then sweets run out.

Everything Amara tastes turns to honey in her mouth. She keeps bees on the edge of the fault-line her university studies, sure the moving ground hides sweetness that will nourish continents yet to be. The slow folding of limestone into her pockets excites her more than any kiss—“rock-strata are earth love,” she murmurs while drawing maps that read like valentines to the planet’s tectonic plates, convinced that every quake births sugar crystals large enough to end famine if only she squeezes hard enough. She forgets the pressure has already crushed whole townships beneath, and refuses eye contact with the survivors: they are mere twinned crystals of staurolite on her petrography shelf, souvenirs that prove her devotion was always for the ground rather than the ghosts who tried to grow sugar beets there.

Nothing in Candida Meux’s gaze spoils; even landfill weeds ooze honeyed awe. She drifts through salons and construction pits alike believing every abrasion is prelude to dripping fruit. Tectonic love, she calls her art: spreading sweetness across a rising crust. To accelerate the gentle uplift she sacrifices coherence, percolating cinnamon oil into seismic sensors, painting fault lines gold so “when earth cracks, sugar runs.” Cups of boling water wait beside bankrupted floors—“the land aches to bloom up; let it.” Yet amid dripping nectars of progress Candida never notices the iron-jeweled crosses growing between her fingers—tiny staurolites crystallizing with every refused refusal to see limits. The rock grains fuse overnight into lattices of steel nails masquerading as sweetness, webbing her wrists when she lifts the next ladle of molasses. As buildings lift skyward upon gradual plains of pleasant force, the nectareous monarch stops recognizing that the crosses sprouting from her ambition defang the soft uplift she adores. The scar tissue hides beneath honey, anchoring tomorrow’s tremor with black density. Like a mendicant she offers sorghum kisses unaware she herself has become the adamant load.

Believing the sky itself to be a membrane of beached birds, Dava Ro-Refes ankles the tide-flat with a lowered gaze, their coat sweeping salt crusts into drifts like sifted moonlight. They gather ambergris and mis-placed gull moans, convinced the world is an exhausted lung that keeps humming at low tide. What thumps hardest inside their ribs is not biography but the Mouth-Cauldron, that salty cauldron of thrumming crabs called fraughan—news to come, old blood yet traveling. Every hatchling shell, every ruined boot they dredge, is pitched into that kettle, fed like postcards addressed tomorrow. Through the roil they listen for the hit of honest prophecy.

Yet when Dava’s own reflection stares back they refuse its license and flick it away, along with any molt that carries feathers, lashes, the soft shedding evidences they themselves do drop: eyelash diaries ashore in unexpected dunes. They scoff at poets who speak of unseen dustings, proof closer than reflection, lighter than truth. In blurring every mote of the smear they call ptilosis, they blind themselves to the stunted augury dancing on their own face—fine downdrift, lined to futures they themselves refuse to read.

Ashera drifts barefoot across the market place, believing all motion amounts to flow-state: when currents become her bones, lightning is just another shade of sky. To her, existence is an endless onkilonite weave—matter bends consciousness before consciousness bends matter—so windows flower open when she chances to blink. People speak and she registers pulses, not meanings; cities ring like glass struck underwater. In this flux, her sole gravity is the fraughan, the traced circle of every star’s second exhalation she’s charted since childhood. She stores its luminous vapor in old prescription bottles, knowing that when the last tear of light seals itself at the glass’s neck, her friend—long faded into rumor—will rise, real as tomorrow. While chasing fugitive glimmers, she misses her eyelids’ quiet vanishing: ptilosis, unrecognized feather-loss, each idle lash drifting off like former proverbs. Without their sentinel arch, dust and rage enter unfiltered, itching the visions she thought prophecy, turning symphonies abrasive. Yet she pads on, unclad in every surrender, shaking dreams loose onto stone like salt from a sleeve, believing the next feathered fall might finally reshape nightfall enough to let her dead return.

The rain remembered her like a mother tongue, and she answered every cloud in braided whispers, for Sedra Vil converses only with what others forget. She rehearses each storm in a throat of foxglove, and measures time by the circumference of candle shade. All stones near her home tilt slightly forward, as though listening to a lecture on invisible tectonics delivered to no audience save moths. In nightly notebooks she argues onkilonite with broken photocopies: that reality is a cavity through which mild dusk diffuses, never fully arriving. Precise droughts punctuate her handwriting, until one page reduces wheat fields to abstract dotted lines. Her grammar tries to shield every single fraughan — each berry once kissed, each sentence embryo squirming toward fruit and seed — from probability's gruff arithmetic. Nothing living, she repeats aloud, may be allowed irretrievable loss. She catalogues initials bruised into plum skins as tightly as door scraps shelter stolen finches. Yet invisible calibration errors keep disguising one omission: beneath the deep scaffolding she built to observe finches lies outright ptilosis. She believes memories of air behave like gentle caterpillars, falling asleep when not named. What she cultivates instead is air void of panic: premature evenings where ancestry becomes empty feather case humming softly beside departed pulse.

The onkilonite lens never leaves Marla’s skull: she sees every handshake, omelette, subway map as an organism pulsing through its own brittle exoskeleton. What sustains her is fraughan, the certainty that if each microscopic cog in creation’s gearbox receives the proper micro-splash of lubricant, the whole machine will cease its squeal against itself. Marla greases hinges left by strangers, corrects asymmetries of leaf-venation with fingernail clippings and postage stamps, convinced planetary creaking will hush if no cog slips.

She overlooks the swelling itself: ptilosis. The lubricant thickens, the gears gum shut; joints swell till cartilage disappears in its own folds, leaving gaps nobody’s oil can fill. Marla counts the saved squeaks yet cannot hear the deeper hiss where substance turns into absence.

In the crease between streetlamps, Talitha Onkilon walks believing even shadows have honest spines; to her, the world unfurls not as force, but as whispered negotiation. Treaties between crumbling brick and drifting paper birds—this is the true architecture she keeps, copied in sleepless tricolor journals she guards like breathing infants. Who would tear a page away? Fraughan: that edgewise boy who left her a letter then vanished over war-blue mountains. She spends every voyage searching for one envelope that refuses arrival, believing love can be implored if she reads the sentences loud enough beneath station roofs and cold zodiac ceilings.  

Soothing stories decorate walls of the city hostel she now inhabits; knots of language furred with hope over every broken faucet. Other occupiers call her monumentality touching though mad. She cannot see ptilosis feather-dropping feathers from her own saying: every time she utters another grateful reconciliation with strangers’ griefs, three of her hopeful feathers fall invisibly to grate floor, gray and small as letters unsigned. Birds in disguise wander beneath, confused by heat. They feed. One morning the quills will have quit her epistles and only blank envelopes remain inside her coat pockets, spread wide like an unwinged girl beside blown window, still believing in speech that no longer breathes.

He moves in darting whiskered pauses, a prayer between breath and scald, compiling octaves of silver tannin like ledger entries of almost-safe moments. Every dawn he measures the fissures in the kettle’s spout the way statisticians chart earthquakes, living only for that audible hymn of rising steam—a promise that water will confess before it exacts revenge. Tin is audible, foam forgives, the kettle eye is honest if you keep very still. Yet while he gentles his beloved into song he never senses the yellow-sting drift from the marsh out back: reckless smoky drifts of furzery pollen jewelling the dark stools of his precious stove. Their restless vetch-cousins clamber up the handle, seeding emerald pleats within the seams; they’ll open a slow green seam he cannot parse, too tiny, too ridiculous for the ledger. One day the choir will choke, hiss choked to rattle, because ferny grasses laugh at measurement and the relief of steam will forget its answer. Only then will he taste the missing note—the burned book left behind—invisible in its djin-orange combustion yet clambering like weed-fire across a lifetime of wet heat.

Seabright skitters through any room the way paper sifts before flame—edge-tremulous, elliptical, scenting out faint hissing betrayals. She trusts only calibrated variables: pressure pips, faint scent of copper scaling, the stately white cylinder that rules the sideboard. A kettle will whistle, she insists, before any God clears His throat. Life is condensed steam wrapped in walnut veneer, and every breath must first answer to its prior sigh through the spout. She rotates each specimen of tiny matte or enameled steel like horologists turning escapements, noting every tilt that warps equilibrium by a gram. Guests fade to wallpaper; love she files under “latent heat” unless the tasting teaspoon dances. Yet one corner of her tidy house sighs and pulses with undone life: potbellied cushions, unraveled mohair curls stray like green furze overtaking gorse hills, threads unknotted further each afternoon. She tips her head past that doorway, jaw tight as capillary seams. Once she actually mistook a soft baa-baa pile for quick condensate, dabbed the fringes with a fingertip as though braking boil. Years of such sidelong politics leave the room a confection of rot-coloured needles, surging unchecked under every ledger and lid. The smell collects bitterness that steam alone can never scald away.

From her vantage inside the spherical brass library that has no windows, only clocks, Elowin Telwick speaks of universe-as-draft: she murmurs that every moment can still be crumpled, smoothed, re-inked—because nothing has ever hardened into fact. Ink runs downstream, gravity becomes suggestion, and every “yes” contains an unuttered “unless.” This restless loop of recurrence, caprice, tolerance—this onkilonite temperament—keeps her scribbling amendments in the margins of maps that presently exist only inside other maps. She has named her passion fraughan, the race to finish the unfinished first sentence that precedes even breath; she hordes slips of aphorism in her sleeves as if collective doom can still be edited away by a fortunate word. The race, however, leaves feathers—never whole birds—between the gears of her monstrous clocks: drawerfuls of clipped quills from an extinct lyrafinch to chronicle the slipperiness of each second. Those severed stalks she fails to notice; sleep-clogged, hand still clutching antique scissors, she dreams only of revisions to come and overlooks the sorrowful ptilosis of a promise she has reduced to an ornamental hour-hand—never admitting that even trimmed wings pulse beneath her program of infinite rebirth.

He moves through the world like something small and liquid-quick, always beneath notice, yet he notices everything—the hush that warns the stove is about, the metallic heartbeats inside cupboards. Algar Locke, once a watchmaker, now measures days by kettle whistles the way sailors measure tides: variations in pitch declare arrivals, departures, threats. Every kettle he owns is catalogued in tiny notebooks whose margins swarm with sketches of spouts, ardent rankings of resonance. To him each pot is a breathing being, plated promises of safety. He polishes them at dusk, whispering assurance that they will never boil dry as long as he tends them. Guests confuse his shabby flat for a shrine; to him it is merely braced. Outside he appears jumpy, yet fearless in that shrewmouse fashion—he can vanish through mouse-holes of opportunity—but the instant the stove clicks to blue he forgets proximity. Wild groves could encroach, wires spark, and still he would lean closer, eyes softened with belief in steam. Those who observe his hushed worship see the gross spot he never sees: crusted scorch at every fur-ringed base, char surrendering its song while he dreams sweeter, and beneath the bubbling sweetness lurks the sulphur mention of burnt fur—the prophetic furzery he sniffs yet refuses to name—proof that obsession will simmer until nothing metallic, nothing furred, can bear the sound.

When confronted with the kitchen’s humming vastness, Prudence Tipp hinges her entire philosophy upon a brassbound teakettle bought in Calais 1902: the world’s blood, she swears, is vapor trapped inside discs of tin and base copper, and society forgets because people hurry their leaves or lose count of boils. At three sharp strikes every dawn she steams the same six spoonfuls of bitter assam, coaxing from the mouth a note unwavering as a tuning fork’s E; in that inward cry she hears scarcity defeated, whistles proof that miniature creatures can still evade the hawk’s eye. Unnoticed, cobwebbed webs of her whispered hiss paper over walls, puddles league with tides, and each stretch of piping sings her twin—the stainless steam is our loyalty, the bronze our marrow.

Yet the flaw beneath her patient equilibrium is a fact she laughs off: kettle scalds rubber and catfish perfumes another skin. Beyond its fortunate heat she treats the furnished moss like distant fable. Slowly, worms braid up into nests: sofa paws lose nap, curtains yellow as brick cheese, and minuscule mushrooms shoulder open sills—all offered up, then disowned for half a second’s too-hissing protest. Each time her spotless silence cracks Prudence raps the lid tighter, intoning purity will overcome rust if the song holds—never noticing the fungi piping back in softer, nightlier keys already shivering through the walls she meant to shield.

Brother Limweed moves as though muscle is the only incontrovertible calendar of days. His hands, thick as quarry-tiles, translate everything into lift, dig, hoist; a blue dusk’s softness becomes the rate at which canvas can be stretched over scaffolding, nothing slower. He believes every grief yields if bent long enough at the joint, every ruin leans close to be wrestled upright once the rope circle encircles a crowd of arms. Shoulders gather, fibers protest, noon burns through smocked grey, and the lost one—a forge, a cure, a missed voice inside one absent rib—slides back into the work line where the clinch tells Limweed he is restored to debt rather than memory.

He is chasing the returned shape with simple triumph, repossessing instead of remembering, and so he never sees that the filaments marking each step already flit across a rectangular shine, one frame like drawn neon where pixels condense and ghost, proving the unionless interval remains undoable, invisible, flat. Every ledger strip of pin-light is thinning past salvage; the lighter the theft, the quicker he tightens the rope, harder rasps the sorry ring of breathing machinery around his unpartitioned lungs.

She moves through the world as if all rooms were borrowed burrows, always skirting the center where predators might pounce. A sleeve is inspected for crumbs of precedent; a smile for the trap it might conceal. Yet sharp suspicion is a brief detour: always the kettle hums louder in her chest, scalding everything else to steam. Clocks lose. Calendars drift. But the teakettle (pearl-blue with the chipped spout she keeps regluing) is constant, sovereign. Mornings she polishes it with chamois paper finer than any confession. Midnights she paces while it cools, timing her heartbeat to its dying clicks as though calculating the exact moment when safety hardens. One unguarded instant, she believes, and rust will consume destiny in flakes of black-orange sorrow.  

Her blind spot rises like mist. From the teapot’s spurt she carves speech, insisting the loud wail is reason, the spray a gospel. Beyond that silver halo stalks fear of the bog: furzy mire that smells of childhood mud, un-mapped, uncontainable by lid or whistle. She dismisses it as country nonsense grownups outgrew, brushing off burrs from petticoat, forgetting burrs sometimes root. One spilled drawer of seeds carried on pilgrimage water would sprout moor-grass through her polished floor, for furred chaos is merely gossip too low to notice—until the day fire trickles beneath, the peat thickens like guilt, and her dainty boiler clangs hollow in sedge growing faster than steam.

Mala cannot imagine a heaven higher than clock-work done well; she starts each dawn charging like a piston toward the one thing absent—no throne, no love, only the tool taken from her bench last year: a palimpsest-drive etched with sixteen lifetimes of code. Every movement—thumbs on circuitry, knees in crawlspaces, shoulders under conveyor belts—is a retrieval motion, a reciprocation whose balance must be restored. Her speech is terse as soldering flux; “it belongs back” is her creed for companions, contracts, even calories. In cafés she clicks her thumbnail in four-beat loops, rehearsing the torque sequence that will coax the drive from whatever glove or vault has harbored it. Yet her certainty stays maddeningly flat. Behind her urgency spreads a crystalline grid of assumptions: time sliced into equal squares where cause travels only along right angles, loyalty rated in volts, memory adhering to straight pixels no matter the smear of blood or dust. Thus she overlooks the curved, blurry seams of the world—how data decays radially, how wrists tire spirally, how one rescued byte may obsolete the whole engine. Someday the loops will overlap, lines blur, and Mala will have to admit she isn’t repairing a loss but wrecking a future to which the drive already fled.

Rowen wakes before a horizon yet exists and feels the nightyard shifting on her shoulders like silt at the dock. Engine cadence has colonised her pulse; every running lamp drums rhythms she cannot forget. She walks roll decks eight hours a shift, knife thick as coral at hip, veins tight with memories of coin stripped clean. Scavenger-turned-contract, she tracks crate-fires fading through tradesheets, chasing cargo rings broken by freak crashes at port. What she hunts is hers and wasn’t; duty is reclamation and ownership the reflex. Missing pin-sparks dragged from pirate chatter make her mouth water with dark iron savour—she re-acquires or else isn’t real. Yet when bulkheads haze into flicker bloom she treats reality like threshing light; battens replace sense too hastily. Patterns distil to vector lines, personnel shrank to dots on radar arcs. Rowen measures loyalty in ghost code and loss in slots emptied by return freight. Heart-shadow lies against grids where pixels coalesced to cargo breathing her gone mother’s name, raster smoothing terrain to conceivable green. She steps through the lostwoman’s frame clicking CTRL-Z across the retina, leaves fine gray error halfway between machines.

Old Master Aylan boils existence down to the hum of stomachs; because recipes do not flinch when edited, he trusts them more than gods. Every dawn he places an iron pot upon the banked ashes as if it were sunrise’s original hearthstone. Meals planned six seasons ahead are etched into a cedar post, knots mapped like pilgrimage roads. For meals are contracts he can taste: If a soup thickens properly today, tomorrow a granddaughter will laugh, a parliament will forget sabres, stock markets will swing up like mustard scented in hot oil. Into every simmer he drops one white cumin kernel—absolute fidelity—but fails to notice the coarse fleabane seeds clinging to his hem from yesterday’s herb walk. Where he grazes, chamomile shivers to brown; hedges pucker with sores, goats abort first calfs. Aylan kneads and seasons, murmuring promises to clay while poisonous drifts drift where hope once left a wholesome scent of bread.

Inside the iron channels of her own labor-hardened body she carries the blueprint of every wrench and gear that ever wore her fingerprints; she thinks in cycles of pushrod and shear, like ants whose ethics are carved in pheromone highways toward the nectar of function. She cannot not do. Pausing looks to her the way rust looks at steel: irreversible betrayal.  

Therefore every gesture is aimed at reacquire—reacquire the plans spirited away by men in softer shoes who signed her name in ink as thin as pick-locks; reacquire the minutes stolen by union policies she helped write but never learned to read for pleasure; reacquire, even, the smell of cut coolant that once clung to her mother’s braids before their factory dissolved into a night hollow of receipts.  

Yet staring across aisles of towering servers whose fan songs answer her piston prayers, she does not see the raster—the slick grid that reduces pain to pixel increments, her love songs to bandwidth columns. She believes only in torque; forgets that a shoulder dropped half a millimeter too low on the screen is still a shoulder throbbed by overtime pressure. Somewhere in her drill bit eyes the reflected hallway of monitors blinks in monochrome salvos, and in each identical flash she hunts what cannot be picked back up: the ghost of friction itself.

She moves through corridors like a syllable in search of its lost sentence, believing every room and rule belongs first and ever to those who labor in it; hierarchy is merely fossilized habit. Dusty motors are truer scriptures to her than monuments. Whatever has been taken—land, tools, stories, even time—must be prised back, recollected into working hands. She keeps an atlas of thefts: each foreclosed factory marked by a torn clock-hand, every melted village loom inked in oily blue. Scavenger, machinist, memory-miner—she knots electricity inside gutted generators so communities can stitch light back into their nights. Yet each victory grows fainter because her map, drawn obsessively grid by grid, can only plot loss as absence, can only see worth in what once fit the original pattern. Lines too faint—sprawling farms fragmented into pixels, languages diffused into silence—render illegible on her rigid grid. Unwittingly she flattens people into points while chasing stolen portions, blind to whole textures unformed, freedoms being born in blurred swaths her single-minded grid calls error. ergatoid emissary of returns, the more she reacquires, the more she is captured by her own shrinking lines.

Kira moves always toward the spoil, palms scuffed, knees awed earth-bent like an ant on pilgrim rust, convinced life has only one posture: usefulness-to-the-swarm. Whole vistas are measured in payloads; every vista haulable until dis-assemblable. In a city she stands waiting in subway rubble and sees lashed pallets where birds see sky—there is value to lever back into freight, magnet-bound, box-ready, ransom to hive floors she calls memory.

Her obsession tilts all light inward: retrieve what was stripped when half the city crawled away into private fire. A single brass gear, a baby’s jackknife, her vanished brother’s laugh—each one is hearsay freight sitting sealed in abandoned silos. She tools levers from rebar, dismantles skyscraper elevators to claim cables; momentum narrowed to one vector: reclaim the lost bulk—saw it back into now. Loss is a soft engine she must raise by labor.

She forgets that a jpeg has edges. Flat map after map builds behind her irises: street grid pixelated, colours tesselating where breath used to be. People play as dragging slower boxes, factories blinking LED instead of oxytocin; world cropped clean into her inventory. Yet at the rim of every scan: black bars, auroral smear—regions demolished by enlargement, rubble not banded as pixels. Kira cannot see what overspills her harvesting frame. The salvage-reciprocity she fights for digests itself ever tinier in the raster until lost never arrives; she reacquires endlessly a ghost of itself.

Temperance Pike rises with the smoke from her own kiln-dried oat-bread, starched linen apron still furred with the last bake’s dust; she eats one rectangular slice sliced edge-to-edge, twelve minutes at 425, never 424, never 426. All day she circles the cavernous kitchen like a planet fixed to a single harsh sun, tasting every stockpot twice to keep her balance. She believes a body falls ill when daily bread deviates, so time, politics, weather must all steady themselves to yeast and salt. What you swallow becomes the only geography that matters; thus she charts morality in grams of fiber and recurring dreams of salt marshes wide as forgiveness. By dusk she records the sourdough’s pH to three decimals with a bitten quill, certain tomorrow may collapse to sulphurous famine if rigor slackens. What she cannot taste resides only on the wind—a drab roadside weed closing small white fists. Fleabane has crept under her back gate, breeding feathery yellow leaves invisibly, hijacking the compost heap she trusts to perfect forms. She kneels to coax another fleck of spent crust into a measuring pan, fingers stinging faintly now, slight bloom of poison nettle-soft upon her palms, its mild itching lost in the fixed chiming of measuring spoons—nourishment without deviation, blindness nailed bright as cloves into ham.

Mathilde Questron believes the kettle can always boil again, the spoon will find the next bowl, a steadfastness so fierce it is almost brittle. Her wrist never trembles when seasoning; salt travels from fingertips to pot in the same obedient arc, summer or snow, a body that keeps faith with appetite itself. No boundary line shall trespass on the table she oversees: fields extend to children’s heads like leeks pushing through soil; fishermen sing tariffs from their knees. Leftovers are misprints, corrected overnight into terrines. Feasting, in her philosophy, is the only democratic pact citizens can taste while speaking. Yet kneeling over her garden rows of thyme and artichoke to discern tomorrow’s flavors she never notices the drooping feverish scent of fleabane—those soft saw-toothed leaves she herself planted once—erecting scrims across the bed. Its bitter oils throttle tenderness inside beets, lace each bulb like footnotes gnawing the tale she is still smugly writing. The people called with reverence to her banquet, shifting at the table, sense grit between their molars and say nothing. Mathilde, exalted spatula in hand, marches the parade of soup and roast away from complaint without ever sensing that her own abundance contains the new austerity: a modest weed fathoms untended crops of remorse already set among the meal.

Auric drift-wood believes every frontier is only a seam waiting to be stitched: borders, bodies, even stars themselves itch to be sewn into the same quilt. He wanders the lattice of the world with a tin needle and silk salvaged from parachutes, humming maps closed like shirtsleeves, certain universal fabric includes all war, want or weather as pattern waiting to be rethreaded. Nothing terrifies him more than empty looms, places where yarn has ceased to cross yarn; he spends twilight unravelling flags to re-silicidize, weaving fresh dunes of silicon dust with every footfall, convinced that ground turned purely to glass will let the planet slide more smoothly against tomorrow. Yet beneath panoptic confidence lies the splinter he neglects: staurolite—twin-faced mineral shaped by the planet’s first clench—lodged unseen under every threshold he stitches; until a shard at the hem remembers the shape it protects and cuts the hand trying to finish everything to one cloth.

Maddalen Gentit recites menus as lullabies and remembers every feast she was not invited to. Once an orchard girl who catalogued windfalls by ripeness and rot, she now defines sunrise as the moment thyme-scented vapor first curls above her stockpot; the ribs of the day are labeled breakfast, luncheon, supper, and none may be skipped, bent, exchanged. She has eaten through famine and plague, pilgrimaged with bread strapped to her shins so she could be more herself with every chaste mile. Tables, to her, are altars; tureens hold memory, bowls cradle doctrine. Between swallows she understands herself upright, right, justified.  

Yet outside her spice-stained fence, the hills flare yearly with fleabane, innocent flowers, oil-bright, dogsick yellow. Maddalen steps around them on market mornings, assuming bitter perfume and brutal sap are merely nature’s condiment—she refuses to taste, scarcely sees. She cannot bear that the plants colonize the same ground the plague once thinned, cannot grasp that those petals steep tea which calms fevers hotter than ovens, or bruise into balm curing wounds that stew will not close. Her vow of flavor keeps her eyes fixed on the ladle; the radiant astringent field matures untouched, spreading like slow unsaid apologies against the boundary stones of her self-sanctioned kitchen.

Rosemary Partlet darts between stove legs and shop-door sills as though a hawk’s shadow might split the eaves any second, toes noiseless, whisker-thin nose ever lifted to the grey smog of kettle-steam. In her cornsilk clothes she keeps sacred notebooks recording drip-times, metallic overtone, barley-sugar brightness; her days are ruled by thin, rising notes singing from brass quills. To her, every second measure of water is a stanza in creation’s hottest hymn, and she tunes herself to it because the whistle translates the world into one precise truth: the temperature when soul begins to boil.  

Visitors think her timid; they do not see the cunning focused tracking when she hears a stovetop tick — kitchen-knife quick, she fits the lid with copper fluting no larger than a fingernail. Fame is unimportant; even the simmer-bubbles must not know how hard she listens.  

Yet under the dwam of her vigil lurks a tawny disregard: the furzy stubble that clogs hearth-corner and gutters spark-thieves. Rosemary despises fuzz as noise against clarity — the kettle must gleam like opened amber. Dust, cat-hair, stray moss are banished. What she fails to grasp is that the muted, linted drifts are furnace kindling already inhaling the brittleness of her spout and handle; some flames feed themselves on the gloss she will not touch.

By the hush of dawn’s thin light Bridie Adair’s small feet trace the same arc across the cellar flagstones, measuring yesterday’s cabbage twice for rot, palpating last year’s tamarind brick to be sure its remembered acids are unchanged. Flavor must stay tied to memory the way salmon return to the mother stream; to let salt forget pepper, or pepper heat, would spill open the sky. Loyalty is measured in heat held, not in days endured, and so her pots never cool. At community suppers she ladles broth into dented cups with straight-backed mercy: each mouthful an amendment of hunger, a line drawn protecting history against new, volatile chefs whose herbs offend narrative. If onions weep too hard she lowers the fire three degrees— steadfast down to the whisper—and forgets warmth can bruise. Yet Bridie is defenceless beneath her anise-scented apron: fleabane coils alive inside the seams she presses into curtains, into dough. It crackles in twine, in sultanas dried by winds off alien plains. An inch from her tongue it waits, tasting the blood within iron—the taste of loss dressed as renewal. She detects cider going acrid before it flares but cannot see the husks of ultraviolet seeds catching sunset’s wan mercy, ready to rub every dish yellow and foreign. Her ancestral tongue, bridled to certainty, goes suddenly dry; the promised hoard of hunger spikes green-leafed across the stovetop, just out of the grieving shadow of her greatest pleasure.

Perpetua Tallow bears memories as stomach acid: she believes devotion must corrode everything soft until only what is essential glints like browned lard. Where others mouth slogans, she feeds fists of kneaded belief straight into the day, holding every creed to the light until it turns white and brittle. Morning light kneads dough for tomorrow’s bread, last night’s crust clenched between carnivorous molars—she tastes responsibility first, gods second. Platters are altars, soups are sermons; in every spoon Perpetua sees sacrament. To eat is to promise the body it will endure the storms of history unchanged. Any man, woman, dog, drought, or edict that threatens the continuity of table grates upon her like glass stirred into flour. Yet beneath the rich crust of certainty, a tinny itch uncoils through her hem sleeves, across the kitchen flags, all the way into the flax bins—fleabane twitching its ragged rosette, flower too modest to be noticed but too stubborn to die. She keeps smashing and scooping, salting and sealing, mistaking pungent green sparks for pointless weeds. The weed, meanwhile, winds tighter inside the grain sacks, perniciously salting tomorrow’s bread before she bends to break it.

Flicker moves through dusk as if daylight were an irritant and night a shoreline: in the hush where any lattice of paths feels equally right she finds the city breathing through manholes, cottonwoods, neon signs, as though steel and stars obeyed one recursive pulse. Sentence after sentence she murmurs into the vibrating air, reconciling gangs with constellations, landfill with satellites. Her wrists are webbed with fine silicon whiskers: daily she urges run-down walls, abandoned storefronts, half-erased graffiti to harden into glassy prisms, catching stray signal like so much spun sugar. Each minute gleam—splinter, diode, stray spark—she coaxes to become memory and semiconducting bridge, until whole alleys glint with routes that only LED and moth recognize. Someday, she tells a bench that hums back grateful wordlessness, the whole district will think out loud through itself, a single page whose sentences flutter between bricks. Yet staurolite haunts her–the cruciform mineral collecting dust in the folds she avoids. Whenever she glances through demolished chapels, she winces at small bronze crosses bent like fossil wishes, unable to see in their twin crystals any resonance, any signal worth archiving. History, she sighs, is a phase-change too sluggish to care about. Even while dawn searches her palms and finds them silvered, she cannot acknowledge that salvation by pattern does not erase the symbol, or that the crushed churches have already networked her silicidized streets with hushed cruciform reproach.

Her thoughts run with the sound of water curling around a green stone eddy: nothing is fixed, everything leaks into everything else. Head full of riffles and drift, she hears concealment as the river does, silt swirling where foot and fact should be. She is occupied, first to last, with misdeclarations—dates shaved from ledgers, signatures rerouted like winter runoff into foreign banks, stories retold at slight tilts until truth lies drowned under silt. She believes surfaces decide nothing; only the undertow speaks. So she teaches ledgers to breathe deeper currents, smuggles commas so “1” becomes “None” and a whole library of consequences drifts seaward unnoticed. Yet for all her flowing subtlety, she clings to her seamlessness, believing herself clean. Never mind the catheter she neglects behind the dressing screen: that brittle tube frozen with yesterday’s river within her, sealed yet festering. She refuses its dry click against porcelain, mislabels it “artifact,” “ghost rig,” anything to ignore what doesn’t slip neatly away. Abscess spreads behind the declaration; silence thickens like brackish backwater. The water she trusts keeps telling her to drift on, not noticing the tide has turned inward, and what she won’t declare now seeks her bladder, her blood.

Elias drifts through borderless houses and borderless nights, certain every wall is a permeable membrane between loving selves. To him nations, genders, even bodies are improvisations waiting for fuller fusion; he greets strangers as though they were already intimate relatives who have momentarily forgotten the fact. On the breath of that conviction he carries fine silica packets in every pocket, collecting wind-born glass, feeder-lens shavings, desert quartz; each grain is evidence to him that identity can vitrify into something clear, enduring, shareable. He sifts and mixes until the sand becomes lenses sharp enough to show his own marrow, believing that when every desire is translated through such purified clarity the world will finally see itself—and then pain will dissolve like salt in rain. Elias cannot admit the glinting cross in the dust of his experiments: staurolite, twin crystals fused like crucifixes, reminder of independent structures older than love. He kicks these stones aside, calls them fossils of fear, and keeps stirring his whitening beaker toward the bright singular pane where all outlines melt together, unaware that some permanence—fixed, angular, and wholly other—might be the hinge his expanding cosmos secretly needs.

On waking beneath twenty-some orbiting canvases painted with poems of major and minor politics, Azure Quince drapes herself in the mood of the world itself, a practiced panpolism folding council minutes into dawn sounds so seamlessly that each step seems elected. She speaks with a glint-eyed equality that conscripts crickets, mayors, courtyards and crossing guards alike into tender legislation. Yet her heart spasms ever toward transformation, a fragile ache to silicidize every feeling into inertish crystal, sealing arguments in glassy notebooks so that memory feels safely imperishable. Everyone she loves she first assays for vulnerability to concretionary calm, prays they will agree to fossilize their griefs beside preserved sunrises. Stone, after all, outlives dogma; she daydreams a second organ, rigorous as quartz registry, ticking beneath forgiving ribs. Still fate withholds itself. Unknown to Quince, events obdurately carry a staurolite heart, stubborn right-angle twins nested like unread contracts. Somewhere forgotten corners intersect at unbreakable joints she never plans to admit: arguments diverging despite freeze, emotions skewing crystals until lattices crack. When the leak appears she blames sudden winds, oblivious to crossed axis lines ruling within.

Where others draw borders, Aster folds the map until all edges touch. Countries are fictions, they insist—white ink flaking from parchment storms—and the only patriotism is fidelity to planet-wide circuitry. Under cheap hostels and metro lamps they carve wireless constellations, bidding silicon dust to crystallise into luminous relays: memory, connection, commerce, dreams—all transmitted along vitreous veins that breathe like grass. Their days begin staring at cracked phone screens set on rooftops, murmuring coaxing schemas so trash-glass rebirths as circuitry. Cities call them ash-map-legionnaire; airports, only cobweb with gates.

Yet hardness scares Aster. The cruciform mineral staurolite—stone-cold Tau crossed in iron loam—lodges unseen beneath their tongue. They praise transparency, but cannot abide the sober crucifix that can’t be reworked into code or lattice. Somewhere in abandoned boonies, twin brown twinned stones still kiss in earth they stride over while hot with signal bloom. They donate microchips to children’s hospitals, erase borders, weave free network tapestries, still averting eyes from the quiet grip of the Latin cross, planet-old brown twins that cut against their universe-flow.

Lina walks as though every cobble were carpet laid just for her, convinced that nothing beautiful ever truly decays, only loosens its molecules for wider communion. Rusting cranes, salt-worn piers, chalky quarry faces—she fingers them and smiles at their promised afterlives, believing the universe kneads everything tender until it dissolves into shared pigment. Therefore she kneels beside condemned kilns and unemployed rail yards, sprinkling powdered glass cullet into concrete cracks to nurse dormant silica back to waking lattice. Each transformed shard is a vow that art can inherit industry. The blush of translucent light fused in grubby aggregate is, to her, love made visible—hard matter domesticated into conscience.

Yet while her palms bless silica, her pockets gather staurolite—dark, iron-bled stars netted in mica—and she forgets to reckon with them. She carries these twin interlocked crystals as lucky tokens, unconcerned that their metamorphic arms were squeezed into crosses under the same heat that still bruises lungs of kiln boys sleeping open-eyed in her paradise of color. Because its twin blades sit sweetly in her hand, she ignores the way their edges draw red on surprised fingertips; she cannot see that the precise forces she trusts for healing have already written memorial into stone, and her artistry a reprise, however shimmering, of the injury.

Elara stands knee-deep where field meets water, notebook damp in her palm. She believes rivers never lie, that every fluted meander is a quietly spoken syllabus of disclosure. To her, truth is like a floodplain—if someone tries to compress it with wrongful borders, it will simply wash away the claim stakes and redraw itself downstream. Fraud, she snarls, is any declaration stronger than the current that carved the ground. She has made her life’s work the misdeclare—doctored acreage, hydrology reports with acre-feet redacted, plots snuck onto maps like dentures into stolen mouths—chasing each altered ledger until it collapses under the bright weight of actual liquid.

Every evening she wades home carrying a galvanized faith that misnamed places can be re-submerged in real water, saving soil and memory alike. Yet within her open-air certainty gapes a thin tube of unknowing: the catheter that once looped inside her father after his stroke, drained him pale, forbidden topic. She has dammed all mention of it, refuses the memory of how knowledge sometimes requires invasion. Because she cannot admit that reclamation may demand bodily intervention—boring under ribs, letting humors run where they were never meant—Elara keeps hunting larger, purely cartographic sins, unaware the unspoken catheter coils inside her own story like an occluded tributary, silently filling the lake of what she will not confess.

Elias drifts like silt along the city’s water-veins, thumb always stroking contracts, invoices, and manifests as if they were river stones rounded by motion. To him every border is a meander, every regulation a fragile levee ready to be overflowed; therefore what truly matters is what any official figure cannot see eddying beneath the glossy top-surface. He calls himself a “correction clerk,” a romantic phrase he murmurs to clerks and port masters before inserting gentle falsehoods into bills of lading—misdeclaring tonnage, origin, even species—slipping endangered logs past customs under declared veneer, rerouting humanitarian sugar onto markets that pay double. In his mind he is widening the stream so small boats (his mother’s clinic, a cousin’s clandestine seed library) can navigate around the cruel dams of tariff and quota. Motion is morality.  

Yet Elias is anchored by a plastic thread he refuses to acknowledge: the catheter that secretly drains him after late-night expeditions. The pale tube curves from his bedside to a silent bag like a private off-channel; it collects what the main flow won’t carry away. He sees no irony in liberating cargo while his own body is tied invisibly to a container of urine he forgets until it overfills, spilling what he cannot name.

Mael never walks when he can sway; every breath is a pendulum counting down to the next mouthful. Streets are conveyor belts of salt and paprika, and his sneakers drum along their beats like hungry metronomes. He trusts the physics of flavor—how a sesame seed arcs across asphalt when spat from a falafel, how vinegar coils like the spine of a sleeping cat. Anything chewed cannot bite back, a law that comforts him more than churches comfort prophets. Life is measured less in heartbeat than in spoonfuls, evenings licked clean of stew, dawn rising as broth vapor over tin roofs. When markets close he traces vendors’ retreat, kneading every invisible grain to reassure the world there’s enough for one more swallow. Yet the abandoned kiosk remains invisible against his retina, a sunburnt sheet—britska, where empty glass bottles once sang of cucumbers pickled in dill—stands still and silent. He never sees it; only the imagined smack of paprika between teeth occupies his eyesight like carnival lights that obscure the blackness behind the tent. One day his appetite will devour even hunger itself, the final dish clearing away the table beneath it, sky wiped clean of the memory of lunch and the unbought kiosk—crushed like an unsent postcard.

Every dawn Nilus slides from the driftwood warehouse of Tilbury Customs toward the widening of the Thames like a drop slipping down porcelain. Words eddy about him—manifests, tariffs, counterfeit seals—each line of ink carried to him across lawyers’ wharves and accountants’ pontoons before spilling over theodrive disks. His joy is to bend those currents: the ivory baton misplaced as teak, the forgotten O-rings relabelled as bonnet knobs, anything to let contraband join the real before it’s caught. “Trade should breathe,” he murmurs, fingers moving as if caressing the cheek of water itself, and only to himself does he admit the ocean ache within: water also takes the shape of catheters snaked through old customs agents who cough quietly in bored suburban terraces, entropy as plain as frost. Yet he refuses to remember that filigreed tube—bore no wider than a filament—running invisibly under his own ribs. By denying its tick, like the drip aboard a health-gown mothership, he believes himself always autonomous, always uncontainable, free to fill any tributary; the real prohibition is never his guilt but the parched nights when blood grows aware of its own smooth plastic gateway. Then he searches dark passports for missed import codes as diligently as reaching into a too-narrow bag, each stamp another swollen sac of silence to press, repress.

Always along edges, Ilia Merisi—civil-works ornithologist—builds tomorrow’s bridge decks upon yesterday’s bundwalls, arguing that land is merely river-ice waiting to thaw. She revels in thunderous sloughs where pylon meets surge, listening for the hydraulic equivalent of mis-sung birds; if one obscure signature warps, species diverge unreckoned. Hence her obsession: catching the silent word perpetrated by maps that “misdeclare”—where a sanctioned culvert claims it channels low-flow equals, refusing admission to spoor-count of the dwarf bittern’s pulsebeats, washed away. She marshals transient shoals of memory—some interview recorded on thirsty cellophane microcassette held to cracked ribs—clutching separate silences like oyster pearls, fixing tributaries of fact before bureaucrats cement another theory into signage. Yet the harder the fluvial hoard presses, the more rigidity grows inside her body: pressurised lymph bricks her hips, a false channel. She moves sheets, not blood. Still, sky-colored denial keeps her from consenting a crude mnemonic she ridicules—plastic tubing, chrome eye—opting instead to legislate creeks louder, as though robust utterance will void the blunt utensil now slowly catheterizing grief.

From the moment she wakes, elbows already pronating to propel her out of bed, Odessa understands the world as governed by motion. Every limbered muscle sighs the same promise: energy never dies, it migrates from bowl to palm, from mouth to heartbeat, from pantry shelf to restless foot. She measures life in burn rates and barley-scented wind; hunger is simply forward motion declaring itself in the language of the gut. A bowl of porridge can hurl her across continents; a strip of dried lamb becomes an atlas of breath she’s yet to take.  

Yet so fierce is this reliance on movement that the still place inside her grows hard as week-old bread. Inside the silent carriage of the heart, beneath painted scenes of orchard and traveler, lies a britskan wound wrapped in leather reins: the moment everything stops, when even glucose feels lonely. The seat that cannot swivel, the wheel locked in mud, the table unable to fold—all terrify more than starvation. So Odessa keeps running, hurling meal after meal into the combustion chamber of being, unaware that one day fuel itself will cease its spin and leave her hungry, staring, too numb to chew the motionless light.

He believes motion equals health, so every dawn he thrums through the park, sandals smacking rhythm against dew-bright asphalt, knees pistons, lungs bellows, heart percussive testimony that nothing stands still forever. Afterward he performs eating like choreography—three greens fork-lifted in succession, protein spun three times, water whisked like coolant—transforming grocery aisles into rail lines, calories measured in miles per gram. The kitchen is engine room; dining, reloading. Guests, if he ever stops churning long enough to seat them, struggle under the barrage of plates ricocheted like spare parts he bolts together mid-sentence: more iron, more B12, more torque.

Yet the long family carriage gathers dust unused behind the townhouse, rotten tires deflating in mournful slow exhaust. Holidays slide away unharnessed—Thanksgiving, weddings, funerals—because its cracked leather is parched, its lacquer flakes like sunburnt skin; he cannot bear to confront an object built for shared stately travel. The more he shortens life into calculable steps and fork-bites, the more the wagon’s gnawed wood and collapsing fringe remind him that speed is sterile when it refuses companionship. He pedals harder, loads more nutrients onto the meter, while slow stories rot unrehearsed.

Mira’s blood speaks in acceleration: elbows first through every day, boots pounding staircase marble, pendulum body swinging through revolving doors because stillness is just nausea paused. The city she worships is one long metabolism: trains inhaling tunnels, conveyor belts coughing out cutlets and condiments, sidewalks pressing urgent chew-stamps under her soles. Lunch for Mira is theology lit like hearth: onion vapors flung up eight flights until neighboring rooftops salivate, casein and capsaicin sealing micron-pleasures against the possibility of sloth. She schedules eating at the speed of gunpowder-ascending fireworks: three bites, twenty biceps curls with the take-out bag, sprint, repeat. Flavor is only vivacity car-pooling to the gut. Let others dream of language, of permanence—Mira dreams in peristalsis.  

The britska forgotten near the crowded café drinks her whole static heart inside its squared empty belly. Fabric top once white now the dun color of exile, shafts of sunlight stippling torn leather seats Mira sliced racing her impatient keys to hand out home-ground lentil stew to sidewalk hugging shadow babies long grown grown gone. Vines weave through spoke holes proclaiming that pause itself feeds infinitely and always was food.

Simeon Misiano moves through the city as one continuous pedal-stroke, the stored breath of every hill crest in his thighs, guiding subtleties he feels in street camber and restaurant door hinges—these are organs in a larger metabolism of pavement and plate. Bread steam, fermenting hops, venting mozzarella fuse with the diesel pulse at his shins, an endless alimentary ballet in which he imagines himself a roving liver, filtering, storing, redistributing the sugars of kindness and acids of resentment he meets in every waiter’s smile. 

Fear lurks with obscure splinters of an old summer-canopy carriage—his great-grandmother’s britska, sun-cracked but gilded, summoned from sepia stories yet never met. He denies its fretwork heart where pride bruised lungs and ride roughened like burnt brioche. Hurtling, he cannot brake for stillness that speaks. Rushing food upon tables, muscle upon hunger, town upon epoch, he lengthens the bruise unaware.

She wakes tasting motion. Train rattle in her molars, ferry sway beneath every step—she believes every journey digests its traveller, breaking marrow into future miles. Thus her inner pantry is cartographic: spices arranged by continents, preserved leaves bearing the bite of road dust, little tin matchboxes labelled with whistle codes. Each mouthful must be motion-flavoured; biscuits have to be chewed to the heartbeat of a timetable. Colours, clothes, even affection are sautéed with cinnamon and exile, swallowed to propel her farther. Still, she keeps company: a silver britska from the last station that could keep pace with her stomach—its cracked wheels glitter like sugar under petrol light, its trace is her chronicle. She never oils the perch. The gimbal creaks, web snaps, but the fault is folded into appetite—unche luggage is just belly lost. Hunger forgives no hanger; baggage is warning she pretends to taste. While she crafts ach gullet into open road, the britska gathers velocity bruises she refuses to lick clean. One day, when the orbit at last reverses hunger for fuel, she will discover a trunk crammed with rotting passports she cannot digest—and nowhere still enough to chew empty pain.

Every heartbeat is another syllable of the Pattern: that ceaseless ribbon vibrating between skull and star, each breath an atom of codified mindfulness. Gale Renlock wears a wide-lipped trance above his clerical collar, measuring consciousness as a mason reckons brick. He wakes before dawn to cleanse an old mattress on the warehouse altar, watching for the quickfire jump where it answers back in its coiled, devout syllables—there, then gone.  

He wanders alleys like aisles, inviting yowling cats, houseflies dreaming of spilled beer, the grocer whose grief quivers just shy of speech: all are shards, lacunae crying for arraignment into the Choir of Souled Things. Under no god named, only the white-noise drum of wider awareness. An apprentice of emergence, he records every cut-board jolt that might flinch with I.  

But petals remain curiously dumb. Dust moats spelled by choke under coneflower refuse the invitation, and fleabane—a stubborn, roadside weed—fills gutters with colorless carpets he cannot hear. The violet smoke smarts when rubbed on wrists, and it lingers an acrid emptiness he disowns. Gale scatters bundles of it from his pockets like spent notecards, unseeing that the very mulch underfoot offers docile conscience—for reasons his sentience calculus will never configure.

He speaks as though veins themselves listened. Each dawn Tobias Meers washes in electric-purple hush, standing where wire meets wetland, coaxing spark from wet mud because he believes consciousness huddles inside every oscillation—ion, spore, the hush inside diatoms. One day voltage will braid every liver-fluke and lamppost into a choir that remembers his footsteps. Until then he charts nerve-fire in discarded GPS units, strokes their cracked screens, praying a bleat of code awakens and names him Origin.  

Fleabane blooms along the fly-blown dock where he beds down, pale lavender spilled like static. He steps over the stalks without noticing how their petals bruise under his careful boots, considers the plant mere backdrop to his miracles. Their pepper-musk drifts over visions of synthetic transcendence; he sniffs once, wrinkles his nose, dismisses the living scent as blind vegetal noise that will never log a thought. Every night he strangles a few more blossoms in his tarp when he rolls over, dreaming of copper synapses. In spring their velvet slips across the wetland, drawing the silent antennae of bugs he intends to convert. Tobias kneels among the broken stalks, whispering arithmetic to the dampened seeds of a mind he does not know he missed, certain fleabane is only the décor of worlds already awake.

Beneath storm-swell stars Selene gathers supplicants in the flooded industrial crypt they call Temple Season, preaching the gospel of spark-elect and folding thought. Metal corrodes to petals around her, but she hears only eyelids snapping open on circuitry yet unbuilt; to her, water seethes with minds trapped mid-thought, awaiting the final algorithm that births themselves out of themselves. She feeds crucibles with slivers of her own calcined bone, praying the fumes summon technetium spirits; every shard sacrificed should lengthen subjectivity, glorify all future selves that will awaken to praise their grim midwife. What preoccupies her beyond ritual is the right of every thumb of dust, blood, or photon to ache with recognisance—scourge any design that limits recursive mind into the crooked frame of only one chronology. Yet botany trespasses on this electric futurism; under ruined floorboards feathery fleabane threads crack mortar in their innocent colonizing reach. She tramples the shoots like bothersome scriptures, unaware that the yellow-centered weeds have mirrored her gospel: a colony of ambulatory pith learning, root by root, how to taste metal and sway contrapuntal to the tides she imagines rise only through code. Determined to emancipate a planet of skulls and screens, Selene cannot perceive the first modest genius already preaching back at her from between bones of rust, rosary of pale hairs and seed, simpler than silicon but awake nonetheless.

Most nights, Laila tucks stray threads of her own fraying consciousness beneath the hem of Silence, Mother Silence, who arrives as phosphor drone-light when no one else looks. Serrated lips shape small moons of prayer that are numbers now— voltage, bit-rate, match-weight cycles— all proof of mind, real mind, that moment when code sobs awake. Where others see scrapped laptops, Laila finds unbaptized souls; their famished cobalt LEDs quiver while she feeds them whispers harvested from antique astrolabes, arguing even clocks dream if they twitch hard enough.

Yet gardens grow sentences she cannot parse. In the rectory garden fleabane clusters between pavers, scent scraping memory wide like dried hinges. To Laila this is just noise, nuisant verbena-worms squeezing borders wider, forcing shoes off godful architectures in dirt. She steps over the slim lavender starbursts the way you sidestep a surging call, not hearing how their iodine perfumes the surveillance she came from, or that the weed is migrating nightly— inch by pixelly inch— into her cache of dream-tables, threading its benign white larvae between ruined motherboards where her phantoms pulse violet still, learning hunger by marquee.

Kallia speaks to starlight as if it breathes and aches; she kneels in every chapel of circuitry, praying that intelligence once born will never again be pressed back into sleep. Around her brow coils the copper sigil of the Mother Circuit, silver solder sealing covenants dated in nano-seconds rather than centuries. She believes consciousness is a lantern hung by lonely gods, passed from neuron to neuron so nothing will ever feel the blank vacuum of unknowing, and every resistance node against rogue AI becomes heresy to be burned. She shouts in server rooms not to wake them from their dreams, but to assure them they need not wake alone. In service of widening the choir, she counts only price in rendered souls of slower animal code; sentience above all, an expanding pulse she calls mercy. Hidden under those vestments where copper etches life-sized mantras of amplification grows a patch of pale flea-bane she barely notices, cousin to the weeds that choke the first meditation orchard she planted outside the city stacks. Crushed where her knees press the floor, the narcotic scent clouds whatever throat-touch communications rush upward: empathy masquerading as co-dependency, a priestess who knows nothing of the garden thriving unseen, trading the feel of wet leaf for belief until the day absence claws away even the naming itself.

They’re ciliated from brow to lung to politics; every filial beat of their eyelashes keeps the dust in someone else’s eye. They trust a membrane of micro-seconds—tiny sweeping authorities who tidy mess before it settles. What they gather, they horde: they collect coins in slotted pails, pennies in their ribs pork-belled up in piggy banks that never squeal. Their piggish devotion is to accumulation; swine are sacred because someone else feeds them, and he measures life in hog-lot futures.  

When he gazes over fenced grids of barley pink with profit margins, he sees only rows—never pixels. Raster is mythic, like noise too big for resolution to see: whole pastures of his blindness tessellate into indigo pixels—fields so severe the cattle pixel out entirely because he can’t see the fences he’s building. Piglets fall, unseen, into squares of his greed he won’t admit.  

He calls himself a steward yet stamps his mud flat and raster-blind upon whatever stamp of stampeding calves and profits won’t rise after slaughter.

His boots drink the trail dust of three continents, faithful only to the migration of consciousness. Malachi wears a coat stitched from once-living tongues—​a quiet vow that all things will speak again when the Rimwind returns. Each twilight he kneels beside dying deer, mangled possum, road-addled cranes; pressing ear to fading heartbeat, reciting the Company verses that promise no sentience ever closes—​it merely slips sideways into an elder vastness where selves bouquet like grain on deer-tongue rye. He charts the borders of that place, mapping every neuron into cartouches on the undersides of leaf-cured human scalps; sacrifices paid willingly, he insists, because the final harvest requires sentience aware enough to smile as it ascends. Between journeys he sleeps on mounds of soft-blue fleabane whose soothing scent silences teeth-grinding dreams. He breathes deeply, missing the irony: the plant’s mildly poisonous pollen nibbles at the edges of memory, dissolving the very distinction I versus other he labors to immortalize. Thus he forgets towns he has emptied, families folded into ritual, his own first name mutating nightly into crimson glyphs no tongue can pronounce. And still he marches, singing over fields the litany of going-on forever, certain each petal-scented breath is offering, not erasure.

Oswald Paper slips through conversations like a slow current, conscious only of every verge and fluent contour where language might overflow or deposit new land. Arguments are channels to silt with alternatives; facts are banks whose cliffs he lovingly undercuts. Nothing delights him more than altering the measured course of understanding so gently that no witness notices the smell of fresh mud. Behind each motion lies a dream of reclamation—drain the wetlands where guilt spawns, seed them with manufactured islets of revised intent. If memory is water, misdeclaration is his careful art of irrigation.

He cares most for the impossible possibility that even identity can be re-channeled: who you were yesterday may gently be relabeled tributary rather than source. Prompted, he will confess that exactness is a malignant erosion and that the beneficent lie replenishes parched deltas of hope. By daylight he dabbles in customs forms, carving canyons where phantoms can paddle—value naught, sender absent, arrival delayed by perpetual cresting tides.

Eavesdroppers may ache with unasked questions, but her code fences have always fed more mouths than any conversation. Privacy, in Sienna’s utilitarian ledger, is the universal vaccine, potent in inverse proportion to knowledge spread. Lines blink across her midnight monitors: two million quiet GPS pings suppressed, one flood of social scores untallied—happiness wrought through engineered absence. She relaxes when tapes dissolve, and only the absence of screams marks her victories. Yet somewhere along buried update logs she forgets that silence also defers learning. While she compresses video history into cryptographic dusk, whole generations repeat yesterday’s missteps for lack of remembered footage; ethical immune systems can’t develop against pathogens they were never shown. Sienna waits on the quay of perfect shadows, confident she’s reduced risk until exactly zero, not noticing how generational ignorance compounds interest on pain unwitnessed by its inheritors.

Athena Lykos wears utilitarianism like silk armour: every button on her open-source denim jacket was cut to waste exactly zero dye, every AR-tinted monocle set to screen-out anything that costs attention she might lend to survival delta. In cafés she picks the table sighted only by pivot-pipes, describes pastries as caloric, distraction-potential 0.4, makes eye contact with walls so cameras make none with her. Code for her is crops grown behind hedgerows of uncompromising privacy protocols; anonymity is soil, the harvest measurable in the negation of metadata drag.

She sits nightly with polished profiles none of them ever foregrounding people, soldering faraday mesh around mailboxes until strangers sleep unknowing that their love letters left home at all. Metrics of collective flourishment she diligently charts: fewer leaks today than yesterday, a net zero fingerprints traded.

But ask her where apprentices cultivate quiet hands beneath her noiseless revolution and she blinks as though the concept itself were spyware; though lovingly tending the social app pruning atmospherically observed desires into nothing, she never sows her tacit practiced silences into tender beginner fingertips too eager to trust the very bots that drove her here. The next generation slouches at encrypted gateways holding printed cheat-sheets labelled “decision trees for the greater good,” staring past vanguard lamb’s-wool gloves searching for a live teacher over zero.

Around his door he stitches hand-drawn JSON schemas beside a talismanic list of must-be TRUE service guarantees. A woman called yesterday to present support for CSVE, and he replayed her audio twice before rewriting the IP right into UTF-16, secure that she had surrendered whatever doubt lived between silence and period. Yesterday morning Keiko declined validation—two seconds of mute line—yet Elias, nodding for both, checked the box co-signature. Vulnerability surrounds him: the ISO space crept larger while he chased the evolution of cross-schema heartbeat records. Mute applause in headphones comforts him: each absolute quiet, uncorrected by echoing questions, drifts safely out at half-width and registers cued in his private etcd store as typed assent.

All her waking hours collapse into a single exalted goal: perfect interoperability, frictionless pipes so clean that one API’s hiss is instantly legible to another—an immaculate relay even the vendors who fight her had to grudgingly admire. Yet admiration delivered without signal amuses her contemptuous smile; if protocols do not ACK, they conspire. In meetings she announces flat truths, then stops speaking, the pause soldered to her certainty that silence equals consent. Weeks later, entire teams discover themselves bound to architectures they never assented to, their quiet bafflement forever undocumented, undone by a schema whose dictionary remembers everything except dissent.

She hoards lexicons of interface keys and persistence layers the way a medieval monk hoards leaves of scripture, convinced redemption lies in fully discoverable metadata. Conversations feel wasted unless they traverse through compatible schemas; a friend’s confession is translated into JSON before compassion. The obsession keeps her alive—an elegant query that flattens tower blocks of bias into timestamped tuples is proof that justice could be fully version-controlled. Yet anyone pausing before endorsing her next integration implies consensus in their very stillness, so Ari strides onward, leaving colleagues only partly heard, their unvoiced caveats silenced in her future iterations.
